In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular and cell biological mechanisms that control the formation of caveolar structures and their functional role in endothelial cells.
the role of caveolae and their coat protein Cav-1 in the pathophysiology of the cardiovascular and pulmonary system.
the role of Cav-2 in the pathophysiology of pulmonary hypertension.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Cav-1-F9A mutant does not affect the formation of caveolar structures, but it does affect eNOS activity and blood pressure.
the Cav-1-F 92A mutant is a useful tool for uncoupling caveolae from its intracellular signaling effects in vivo.
this study demonstrates that the F92 residue of Cav-1 is a key regulator of the NO bioactivity in endothelium.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have identified a point mutant of Cavolin-1, which uncouples the protein from its downstream signaling.
we were able to uncouple caveolae formation in vivo from its downstream signaling effect.
Cav-1-F 92A is a mutant form of Cav-1, which retains the ability to form caveolae, but is unable to bind eNOS and inhibit its activity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the F92 residue of Cav-1 is a major determinant of eNOS activity in vivo and that this residue is not required for caveolae formation.
the F92 residue in Cav-1 is a key determinant for the regulation of eNOS.
the Cav-1-F 92A mutant does not interfere with caveolae formation, but it is able to uncouple Cav-1 from its inhibitory action on eNOS and, therefore, increase the levels of NO bioavailability.
